stories.headline: FED HIKE ODDS NEAR A COIN FLIP AS CME FEDWATCH JUMPS TO 46.5% AHEAD OF TUESDAY'S MEETING
stories.body: CME's FedWatch tool now prices a 46.5% chance the Fed raises rates a quarter point at Tuesday-Wednesday's meeting under Chair Kevin Warsh, up from 34.7% a week ago and just 10.7% on July 15, after Governor Lisa Cook flagged inflation running at 3.7% - nearly double the Fed's 2% target - even as a weekend pause in US-Iran hostilities gave oil some room to cool.
stories.explain: FedWatch converts prices on 30-day Fed funds futures into an implied probability: each contract settles on the realized average overnight rate for its month, so when traders bid up the rate the contract implies, the tool's math mechanically spits out a higher hike probability - the near-quadrupling from 10.7% to 46.5% in eleven days reflects real money repricing, not just sentiment. The trigger was a genuine supply shock (oil approaching $100 during the worst of the Iran strikes) hitting an already-hawkish committee, since energy costs feed almost immediately into headline CPI and travel through diesel and freight into core goods within a month or two. Whether Tuesday lands on 'hold' or 'hike,' a probability this close to 50/50 means Warsh's press conference language will move markets more than the vote itself, because half of positioning is already wrong no matter which way it goes.

stories.headline: US AND IRAN HOLD FIRE FOR A SECOND STRAIGHT NIGHT AS TALKS WITH OMAN CONTINUE
stories.body: The US paused strikes on Iran for a second consecutive night and Tehran held off retaliating as diplomatic contacts routed through Oman were described as 'constructive,' with President Trump telling reporters he's giving the talks 'some space' while also denying reports the US is running low on munitions after nearly two weeks of near-nightly strikes.
stories.explain: A two-night pause after 13 straight nights of strikes is the clearest signal yet that both sides see more value in a negotiated off-ramp than further escalation, which is exactly the kind of headline that unwound the war-risk premium in Friday's oil selloff. But de-escalation headlines get discounted more slowly than escalation ones - traders know a single failed round of talks or one intercepted strike can restart the campaign overnight, so oil hasn't given back anywhere near the full run-up despite two quiet nights. Munitions-supply denials matter economically too: if markets believed the US were actually depleting stockpiles, it would read as a forced de-escalation rather than a chosen one, a distinction that changes how much confidence to put in the pause holding into the FOMC decision.

stories.headline: HOUTHI STRIKES ON SAUDI ARAMCO FACILITIES AND IRANIAN SHIP STOPS IN HORMUZ KEEP OIL'S SUPPLY RISK ALIVE
stories.body: Even as the US and Iran held fire directly, Iran-aligned Houthi rebels claimed attacks on Saudi Aramco refineries in Jizan and Yanbu, and Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it stopped four vessels attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz over the past 24 hours - a reminder that the conflict's most market-sensitive chokepoint remains active even during a lull in direct US-Iran fire.
stories.explain: Roughly a fifth of global oil consumption physically transits the Strait of Hormuz, so Iran boarding or turning back tankers there is a far more direct threat to supply than the US-Iran strikes themselves, which have mostly hit military and nuclear-adjacent targets rather than export infrastructure. Markets price chokepoint risk asymmetrically to strikes on land: a single seized tanker can spike freight insurance rates and effectively taxes every barrel that still gets through, which is why Hormuz headlines tend to move oil futures faster than casualty counts from the broader war. Heading into an FOMC meeting where inflation optics matter, a Hormuz incident that spikes oil even 5-10% would hand hawks like Cook fresh ammunition just as this weekend's strike pause looked to be cooling the inflation narrative.

stories.headline: DIMON WARNS MARKETS ARE UNDERPRICING GEOPOLITICAL AND FISCAL RISK AS S&P'S H1 RALLY LEANS ON A HANDFUL OF CHIP STOCKS
stories.body: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said investors are underestimating risks facing the global economy - citing the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, US-China tensions and rising military spending against a backdrop of mounting government deficits - even as the S&P 500 is up more than 10% year-to-date, gains that are heavily concentrated in semiconductor names.
stories.explain: Dimon's warning is really a concentration argument: when an index's return is driven by a narrow slice of megacap and chip names rather than broad participation, the headline number overstates how much cushion the market actually has if any single one of those names disappoints, because there are fewer offsetting winners to absorb the hit. That's the same fragility Friday's BofA Bull & Bear Indicator was flagging at its most bullish reading since 2021 - extreme positioning and narrow leadership tend to travel together, since a rally with few new buyers left outside the winning trade has nowhere to rotate into when sentiment turns. With a near-coin-flip Fed decision, an active Middle East war and a thin-breadth rally all colliding in the same week, Dimon's point is that the market's margin for a negative surprise - on any of the three - is unusually small right now.

stories.headline: ST. JOHN'S LOSES TRANSFER BIG DONNIE FREEMAN FOR THE SEASON TO A TORN ACHILLES
stories.body: St. John's forward Donnie Freeman, who transferred in from Syracuse after averaging 16.5 points and 7.2 rebounds last season, will miss all of 2026-27 after surgery on a torn right Achilles suffered during a non-contact workout injury, a major blow to Rick Pitino's roster heading into the season.

stories.headline: LEBRON JAMES SIGNS WITH THE 76ERS ON A TWO-YEAR, $8 MILLION DEAL
stories.body: LeBron James has agreed to finish his career with the Philadelphia 76ers on a two-year, $8 million contract, a stunning below-market deal that lets Philadelphia keep building around Joel Embiid and newly acquired Jaylen Brown while James chases a fifth ring; the Sixers also added Kentavious Caldwell-Pope on a buyout from Memphis this weekend.

stories.headline: 49ERS COACH KYLE SHANAHAN WILL BE LIMITED AT TRAINING CAMP AFTER A CAR CRASH LEFT HIM WITH A BROKEN NOSE, RIBS AND HAND
stories.body: Kyle Shanahan is recovering from a July 14 two-car accident in Palo Alto that left him with a broken nose, three broken ribs, a broken hand, over 40 stitches and a concussion; GM John Lynch says Shanahan will participate in a limited capacity as camp opens, with assistant Chris Foerster covering head-coaching duties, and the team expects him back well before the Sept. 11 opener in Australia against the Rams.

stories.headline: ARCH MANNING'S FORMER ROOMMATE PARKER LIVINGSTONE HEADLINES CAMP-WEEK TRANSFER STORYLINES AFTER JUMPING TEXAS FOR OKLAHOMA
stories.body: As fall camps open across the country, one of the transfer portal's most talked-about moves remains wideout Parker Livingstone's jump from Texas to archrival Oklahoma - he caught 29 passes for 516 yards and 6 touchdowns as a redshirt freshman and was Arch Manning's roommate in Austin before calling the move a 'business decision' and vowing to 'beat the crap out of' his old team in the Red River Rivalry.

sports.detail: Recruiting focus is shifting toward the 2028 class, with 3-star Puyallup safety Markel Newell seen as a potential first commit, even as Jedd Fisch takes over as offensive playcaller after OC Jimmie Dougherty's February departure. Season opens Sunday, Sept. 6 vs. Washington State at Husky Stadium.

Still quiet on the hardwood as Danny Sprinkle rebuilds after a 16-17 season - Croatian forward Boris Tišma's commitment and Hannes Steinbach's No. 14 selection by Charlotte in the 2026 NBA Draft remain the offseason's headline additions and departures.

Seattle held its second public training camp practice Sunday with no fresh injury news to report; WR Tory Horton practiced Saturday for the first time since his season-ending 2025 shin injury. Coach Mike Macdonald says roughly 30% of the roster has turned over as the champs defend their Super Bowl LX title.

Jalen Duren's restricted free agency standoff has reportedly gained momentum, with the Caris LeVert-for-Prince/Harris trade freeing cap room toward his 25% max (5 years, $239M); Duren's first All-NBA nod this year also makes him eligible for a 30% supermax, and league sources still see a deal landing near $200-220M before it's resolved, possibly stretching into August.

Seattle salvaged game three of its four-game set in Arlington, riding back-to-back home runs from Dominic Canzone and Randy Arozarena in the 7th to snap a two-game skid after Texas had taken the first two 5-4 and 7-1. The Mariners sit right behind the division-leading Rangers in a tight AL West race; the series finale is Monday.

Big Ten Media Days conclude Tuesday-Thursday, July 28-30, in Chicago
Mariners at Rangers series finale, Monday — Seattle salvaged game three 6-4 after dropping the first two
Seahawks training camp runs through Aug. 13 ahead of the Sept. 9 opener vs. New England

deepDive.title: Reading the Fed Funds Futures Curve: How an Oil Shock Turns Into a Rate-Hike Probability
content: Today's brief has three stories orbiting a single number: the probability the Fed hikes rates on Tuesday jumped from 10.7% on July 15 to 46.5% today, an eleven-day move driven almost entirely by oil prices spiking on the Iran war and now partially unwinding as a strike pause holds for a second night. That kind of swing in hike odds this close to a live meeting is unusual - it means the committee itself is genuinely undecided, not performing a decision markets already know is coming. Understanding how a war half a world away turns into a rate-hike probability requires understanding the specific mechanical pipeline connecting futures prices, headline inflation, and a central bank's reaction function.

The mechanism starts with CME's FedWatch tool, which doesn't survey anyone - it backs out probability from the price of 30-day Fed funds futures, contracts that settle based on the realized average overnight rate for that month. If traders bid the contract price down, implying a higher average rate, the tool's math shows a higher hike probability; the move from 10.7% to 46.5% is real money repositioning, not commentary. That repositioning was triggered by oil's run past $100 during the worst of the strikes, because energy is one of the fastest-moving inputs into headline CPI - gasoline and diesel prices adjust to spot crude within days, and higher freight costs bleed into core goods within one or two months, giving the Fed a concrete, dated inflation risk to react to.

What gets missed is that not every oil shock deserves the same policy response, and the Fed's own history shows the cost of getting that distinction wrong. In the 1970s, the Fed treated OPEC-driven oil shocks as one-off price-level shifts and kept policy too loose, letting energy costs embed into wage and price expectations until inflation became self-sustaining - the textbook case for why 'transitory' framing can be dangerously wrong. The 2022 shock cuts the other way: policymakers who had just been burned by underestimating an inflation shock overcorrected on caution, hiking through pain because they no longer trusted their own read on which shocks would fade. Today's Fed, under Warsh, is explicitly weighing which precedent applies to an oil spike caused by an active war rather than an OPEC supply decision.

That history is exactly why Tuesday's press conference will matter more than the vote itself: at 46.5%, roughly half of positioned money is already wrong regardless of the outcome, so Warsh's language about whether this oil shock is being treated as transitory or persistent will move yields and the dollar more than the rate decision does. It also explains why this weekend's news matters as much as the meeting - a genuine two-night strike pause with talks continuing through Oman argues for treating the shock as fading, while Houthi strikes on Aramco facilities and Iran's tanker stops in Hormuz argue the opposite. A single incident in the Strait before Tuesday could still flip the committee's read entirely.
